description: A.M.N.P. (Alliance for Multidisciplinary Network Projects) is a multidisciplinary engineering team dedicated to integrating computer systems, infrastructure design, and environmental sustainability. Driven by collaborative synergy and technical rigor, we build innovative, data-driven solutions engineered to tackle complex aerospace challenges while creating a meaningful, positive impact on our world
summary: Survive in Space is a browser-based educational game for kids. Players command the spaceship Ares on a journey to Mars while managing three resources: Energy, Life Support, and Shielding. The game has four rounds based on real space situations: a solar storm, rover terrain reconnaissance on Mars, solar conjunction (radio blackout), and the return trip home. Each round has a short story, a decision, and a minijuego (mini-game), and every choice has a cost. If any resource reaches zero, the mission fails. The first round pulls live data from NASA’s DONKI space weather database to show the latest real solar particle event. Each round ends with a “Based on a true story” note linking the gameplay to real missions. It turns hard ideas, such as radiation, autonomous navigation, and communication delays, into choices that kids can understand and replay. The game needs no installation or backend.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
The game follows a fixed loop. The player reads a mission report, chooses between two or three options, plays a mini-game linked to that choice, and sees how Energy, Life Support, and Shielding change. Each resource starts at 70% and the game ends in failure if one drops to 0. Mini-games include a power-grid puzzle, a sensor data check, a Mars rover driving, route planning, and radar mapping challenge, an offline-kit packing puzzle, a habitat alarm drill, a shield-defense game, and a rocket launch timing game. In Round 1, the game queries NASA’s DONKI API for the most recent solar energetic particle event and shows its date, instrument, and linked solar eruptions. If the API is unavailable, the game continues with default values.

What benefits does it have?

  • It teaches real space science concepts (radiation, star trackers, autonomous rovers, solar conjunction, shielding) through play instead of lectures.
  • Each round ends with a fact tied to real NASA missions.
  • It encourages critical thinking, because every option has trade-offs in resources.
  • It runs in any modern browser with no account, install, or server.

What is the intended impact?
We want to make space science approachable and memorable for young learners, and to show that real open data can power educational experiences. The game is also built to be extended: new rounds and mini-games can be added by editing data files, so teachers or other developers can grow it.

What tools, languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Language: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML5, and CSS3.
  • Rendering: native DOM and Canvas 2D for the Mars mini-game.
  • Audio: Web Audio API, with all sounds generated in code.
  • Build and quality tools: esbuild for bundling, Node’s built-in test runner for automated tests, and ESLint for linting.
  • Data source: NASA DONKI API (Space Weather Database of Notifications, Knowledge, Information).
  • Hardware: any standard computer or mobile device with a browser, with keyboard and touch controls.

How is your project creative?
It combines storytelling, resource-management decisions, and a different mini-game for each choice, so every option feels different. It blends real NASA data with a game, and each round is inspired by a real mission event. For example, in May 2024 solar storms overwhelmed the star camera on NASA’s Mars Odyssey orbiter. The retro pixel-art look, the typewriter-style “letters”, and the synthesized sound effects give it a distinct identity without any audio files.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Audience: simple English, short texts, and a “Quick science” note that explains key terms.
  • Accessibility: keyboard shortcuts, screen-reader announcements, focus management, and support for reduced-motion preferences.
  • Reliability: if the NASA API fails or is offline, the game keeps running, and results are cached for six hours to avoid repeated requests.
  • Security: the interface is built without innerHTML, so external data is never interpreted as code.
  • Maintainability: game logic is separate from the interface, content is separate from code, and automated tests cover the core logic.
  • Scientific honesty: the game uses real events as inspiration, and the storm-strength rule based on linked solar eruptions is labeled as a game rule, not a scientific measurement.
